subject: physics
question_text: Define simple harmonic motion. Show that the motion of the projection of a particle performing uniform circular motion, on any diameter, is simple harmonic.

verification.note: The mark split is invented and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The question itself is sourced, not invented.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

cuts.label: 4-mark answer
cuts.question_text: Define simple harmonic motion. Give examples.
cuts.note: The Fastrack asks the definition alone as Short Answer 1 and the definition plus the projection proof as Long Answer 2. One authored step list, two lengths.

steps.label: The definition
lines: A body is said to be in simple harmonic motion
if it moves to and fro along a straight line
about a fixed mean position, such that its
acceleration is always directly proportional
to its displacement and is always directed
towards the mean position.
steps.why: Two conditions, not one: proportional to the displacement AND directed back towards the mean position. The minus sign carries the second.
common_mistakes: Stating only "acceleration is proportional to displacement" and dropping the direction — that alone is not simple harmonic motion.

recall.must_convey: That the acceleration is proportional to the displacement and always directed towards the mean position.
accept: a is minus omega squared y

steps.memory_tip: Two conditions, not one: proportional to the displacement AND directed toward the mean position. The minus sign states the second.

steps.label: Examples
lines: 1) The oscillation of a loaded spring.
2) The vibration of the prongs of a tuning fork.
3) The oscillation of a simple pendulum.
4) The projection of uniform circular motion
on any diameter.
steps.why: The fourth example is the one this question goes on to prove — it is not a separate fact but the body of the answer.
common_mistakes: Offering the motion of the earth around the sun; that is periodic but not simple harmonic.

recall.must_convey: Examples such as a loaded spring, a tuning fork, a simple pendulum and the projection of circular motion.

steps.memory_tip: Keep a list of four: pendulum, loaded spring, vibrating string, and the projection of circular motion.

steps.label: The reference circle
steps.why: The circle is called the reference circle: P is a fiction we invent, and N is the real motion we want to describe.
common_mistakes: Drawing the perpendicular from P to the wrong axis, so that N no longer lies on the diameter being studied.

recall.must_convey: That a particle P moves on a circle of radius A with angular velocity omega, and PN is dropped perpendicular to the diameter.
accept: draw the reference circle with P and N
perpendicular from P to the diameter
reject: y is A sin omega t

steps.memory_tip: Draw the reference circle: P moves on the circle, N is its shadow on the diameter.

steps.label: The displacement
lines: Let a particle P move on a circle of radius A
with a constant angular velocity ω. This is
called the reference circle.
After a time t the radius OP has turned
through an angle θ = ωt. Drop PN perpendicular
to the diameter yy′. From the triangle ONP,

lines.text: sin θ = ON / OP = y / A
y = A sin θ = A sin ωt

steps.why: N is the shadow of P on the diameter, and this one line of trigonometry is the whole link between circular motion and SHM.
common_mistakes: Writing y = A cos ωt without saying the timing is measured from a different starting point.

recall.must_convey: That theta is omega t and from triangle ONP, y equals A sin omega t.
accept: y equals A sin omega t

steps.memory_tip: One trigonometry line does it: y = A sin ωt — the shadow of uniform circular motion.

steps.label: The acceleration
lines: Differentiating with respect to t gives the
velocity of N, and again gives its
acceleration:

lines.text: v = dy/dt = A ω cos ωt

steps.why: Each differentiation brings down one factor of ω, and the second one brings back the original sine with a minus sign.
common_mistakes: Losing the minus sign in the second differentiation, which destroys the whole proof.

recall.must_convey: That v is A omega cos omega t and a is minus A omega squared sin omega t.
accept: v is A omega cos omega t
a is minus A omega squared sin omega t
reject: y equals A sin omega t

steps.memory_tip: Differentiate twice: each step brings down one ω, and the second brings back the sine with a minus.

steps.label: The conclusion
lines: But A sin ωt is just y, so
The acceleration of N is proportional to its
displacement and is directed towards O.
Hence the projection N moves with simple
harmonic motion.
steps.why: The proof closes by matching the definition word for word — proportional to the displacement, directed towards the mean position.
common_mistakes: Stopping at a = −Aω² sin ωt without substituting y back, so the definition is never actually matched.

recall.must_convey: That a equals minus omega squared y, matching the definition, so the projection is simple harmonic.
accept: a is minus omega squared y
reject: v is A omega cos omega t

steps.memory_tip: a = −ω²y matches the definition word for word — say so to close the proof.

insider_note: The definition alone is also asked as its own question — learn it word for word.
